title: Population Density Compare: Crowded, Measured
description: Compare population density between places with Population Density Compare — same census, same land-area rule, honest numbers. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Manhattan packs about 74,244 people per square mile (2020 Census) while Wyoming averages 5.94 — a ratio near 12,500 to 1 between America's densest county and its emptiest state.
quick_answer: Population Density Compare sets places' population densities side by side — people per square mile or kilometre — computed from the same census and the same land-area rule for both. Name the pair and read the comparison: density is where 'crowded' stops being an adjective and becomes a number.

“Densest place in America” is a density claim with a denominator problem. This comparison keeps land area consistent so the claim survives the comments section.
Delivery economics, clinic catchments and retail formats all bend on density. Two candidate territories compare here before a model is built.
A state that looks empty can hold a denser city than a 'crowded' rival's — Wyoming's 5.94 per square mile against any city's thousands is the calibration example.

New York County (Manhattan): 1,694,251 people on 22.82 sq mi of land = 74,244 per sq mi (28,666 per km²). Wyoming: 576,851 on 97,093 sq mi = 5.94. Both 2020 Census — the 12,500× gap is real, and it is mostly a story about denominators.

New York City as a whole runs 29,302 per sq mi — Manhattan alone runs 74,244. City-versus-borough comparisons change the answer by 2.5× without any number being wrong: boundaries are the argument, density is the arithmetic.

faq: Both sides of a comparison share the stated census (2020 for the US anchors on this page) — mixing vintages manufactures gaps that are really just growth, and the tool refuses the trick.
Land only — harbours and lakes are not lived on. Total-area densities flatter waterfront cities; the land rule is the honest denominator and it is applied to both sides.
City, county or state — which unit?

Density belongs to whatever boundary you choose, and the answer changes with it (see the Manhattan example). Comparisons must match unit kinds — city with city, county with county — and the table labels each side's unit.
Why is the US average so low?
Most American land is not urban. The average is a real number that describes almost nowhere — density is a local fact, and national means are context, not comparison material.
Both units are reported; the conversion is exact (1 sq mi = 2.59 km²), and European readers get their native scale without re-deriving it.
Censuses count residents where they sleep. Manhattan's daytime density swells far beyond 74,244 with commuters — a different, legitimate statistic that must be named when used.
No threshold exists in the number itself — outcomes depend on housing, transit and services built for the density. The comparison informs; it does not grade.
Tiny denominators make wild densities (a village of 200 on 0.01 sq mi 'beats' Manhattan). Comparisons below a few thousand residents are arithmetic novelties, flagged as such.
